title: Current-based RF charge sensing in a carbon nanotube
authors: Marta Cagetti, Stefan Forstner, Victor Champain, Roger Tormo-Queralt, Christoffer B. Møller, Sergio L. De Bonis, Chandan Samanta, Elsa Vázquez-Rodriguez, Eneko Mateos-Madinabeitia, David A. Czaplewski, Adrian Bachtold
abstract: Ultra-sensitive charge detection is a widely used tool for quantum electronics with applications in quantum information processing and in probing the physics of condensed matter systems. Existing approaches require either an impedance-matched resonant circuit, or millimeter-scale proximity between amplifier and sample, both adding complexity and constraining device design. In this work, we introduce a current-mode charge sensor in a suspended carbon nanotube, operating at the $1.25$ MHz resonance of an RLC tank circuit and achieving a charge sensitivity of $0.15~μe/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. We utilize it to measure a double quantum dot (DQD) electrostatically defined in the same nanotube, revealing a highly regular charge stability diagram. We perform single-shot readout of the DQD charge state at an integration time of $3.56~μ\mathrm{s}$, without any false assignments over $10^{7}$ measurements and a signal-to-noise ratio of 17 exceeding the state of the art.
summary: The paper introduces a novel current-mode charge sensor based on an RLC resonant circuit implemented in a suspended carbon nanotube. This method overcomes limitations of previous techniques by avoiding impedance matching and suppressing low-frequency noise. It successfully measures the charge state of an embedded double quantum dot with high fidelity, advancing solid-state qubit readout technology.
main_problem: Developing ultra-sensitive charge detection methods for quantum electronics applications, which are crucial for quantum information processing.
main_result: The authors achieved a high charge sensitivity of $0.15 \mu	ext{e}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$ and demonstrated single-shot readout of a double quantum dot (DQD) with an SNR of 17, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques.
method: They introduced a novel current-mode charge sensor operating at the resonance of an RLC tank circuit to measure charge changes in a suspended carbon nanotube.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes a double quantum dot (DQD) electrostatically defined within a suspended carbon nanotube, which acts as the highly sensitive charge sensor coupled to an RF-resonant circuit.
key_observables: Charge stability diagram mapping ($\Delta V_{peak}$ vs. gate voltages), single-shot readout fidelity, and current noise spectral density.
important_parameters: Achieved charge sensitivity $\delta q \approx 0.15 \, \mu	ext{e}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$; Resonance frequency $f_{RLC} = 1.25 	ext{ MHz}$; Integration time $	au = 3.56 \, \mu	ext{s}$.
main_assumptions: The sensor remains functional up to tens of Kelvin, although sensitivity decreases; the method relies on converting current measurement into voltage readout at resonance.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate SEM images of the CNT setup, schematics of the RLC circuit, Coulomb blockade peaks in conductance measurements, and frequency response curves demonstrating the resonant operation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for sensitive charge detection. It then details the current-mode RF sensing methodology using an RLC resonator to overcome limitations of previous techniques. Finally, it applies this sensor to map the DQD stability diagram and perform high-fidelity single-shot readout.
why_interesting: This work presents a highly engineered electrical measurement technique (RF resonance) applied directly to solid-state qubits (DQD in CNTs), which is central to realizing scalable quantum computing hardware.
